Salvador Dalí. A Spanish painter, filmmaker, and provocateur who lived from 1904 to 1989 and became the public face of Surrealism, despite ideological tensions with the movement's founder André Breton. Dalí developed a technique he called the paranoiac-critical method, a deliberate approach to irrationality designed to access the unconscious. This produced hallucinatory paintings of melting clocks, mutated landscapes, and doubles that became iconic.

Born in Catalonia, Spain, Dalí trained in classical technique before discovering Surrealism's dreamlike possibilities. His paranoiac-critical method involved inducing a paranoid state to access irrational associations and unconscious truths. The Persistence of Memory, created in 1931 and featuring melting watches in a hallucinatory landscape, became Surrealism's most iconic image.

Dalí excelled at painting dreams: impossible spatial logic, fused forms, uncanny juxtapositions that seem both beautiful and disturbing. His technical skill—his ability to render dreamscapes with photographic precision—gave his hallucinatory visions an uncanny credibility. He became a celebrity personality, adopting surrealist outfits, theatrical public appearances, and a trademark mustache. Art and self-promotion merged.

Controversially among Surrealists, he embraced commercial art, film, advertising, and fashion—anathema to purist modernists who saw mass culture as corrupting. His ideological positions became increasingly controversial: monarchist and religious turns troubled André Breton, who eventually expelled him from the movement. Yet Dalí remained prolific and commercially successful even after Surrealism's decline, crossing into fashion, jewelry, and film design throughout the mid-twentieth century. His legacy remains contested: celebrated as a master of technique and imagination, criticized for commercialism and narcissistic self-promotion.
